item.title: 12 Smart Parenting Practices That Can Keep Your Child from Growing Into a Codependent Narcissist
item.description:
Every parent wants their child to grow up with a healthy sense of self. Although sometimes, without meaning to, we pass along habits that set them up for unhealthy patterns instead. One of those patterns is when a person turns out to be a codependent narcissist.

This is someone who struggles extremely with boundaries, craves approval, and at the same time tries to control others in a toxic way to feel secure.

The tricky part is that these traits don’t normally just start overnight. Typically, they are cultivated slowly, often starting in childhood. That’s why the everyday choices parents make matter.

We’ve put together a list of some smart practices that help kids grow into balanced adults who don’t fall into the trap of codependent narcissistic behaviors.

Teach kids that “no” is not a bad word

Children need to learn both sides of “no.” If they never hear it at all, they may grow up expecting the world to bend to their wishes. If they’re never taught how to say it, they may grow up afraid to stand their ground.

Both extremes feed unhealthy patterns.

As a parent, you can practice this by letting kids say no to small things, like not wanting another helping of food, and respecting it. At the same time, parents should use “no” themselves in a calm, firm way that shows limits are part of life. This teaches kids that boundaries are normal, not punishments.

Praise effort, not just results

Kids who only hear praise when they win or excel start tying their worth to their performance. That’s a fast track to narcissistic thinking. On the other hand, kids who never hear encouragement may grow into adults who constantly seek approval from others.

Instead of focusing only on outcomes, notice the effort. Say things like, “I appreciate how hard you worked on that project,” or “I saw you kept trying even when it was tough.” This builds resilience and teaches kids that their value isn’t tied to being perfect.

Let them solve small problems

It’s natural to want to protect kids from frustration, but stepping in too quickly robs them of the chance to learn problem-solving. Whether it’s a playground disagreement or a forgotten homework assignment, letting them figure things out teaches independence.

Over-rescuing feeds codependency, while over-controlling feeds narcissism. The balance is giving guidance without taking over. Ask questions like, “What do you think you could try next?” rather than rushing to fix things yourself.

Show them what healthy boundaries look like

Boundaries aren’t walls; they’re lines that protect relationships. Kids learn boundaries by watching how parents set them. If they see you respect your own limits – like saying you need quiet time after work – and honor others’ limits, they’ll grow up less likely to fall into codependent narcissist patterns.

Boundaries also mean teaching kids that it’s okay to disagree respectfully. This helps them understand that closeness doesn’t require sameness.

Encourage honest conversations

Kids sometimes hide their feelings because they fear disappointing their parents. Others exaggerate their feelings to get attention, which can all lead to unhealthy habits.

Create space for honest talk, without judgment, so they learn that truth is safe. Ask open questions like, “How did that make you feel?” and listen without rushing to correct or dismiss. When kids know their voice matters, they’re less likely to seek control or approval in unhealthy ways.

Teach the difference between confidence and control

Confidence says, “I believe in myself.” Control says, “I need to manage everyone else.” Helping kids understand the difference keeps them from confusing leadership with domination.

Parents can model this by showing confidence in their own choices without needing to control others. For example, saying, “I feel good about the decision I made,” is different from saying, “Everyone should do it my way.” This distinction helps kids grow into adults who lead without overpowering.

Model apologies that mean something

Parents who never apologize teach kids that admitting wrong is weakness. Parents who over-apologize teach kids that their worth depends on pleasing others. A balanced apology, clear, sincere, and not overdone, shows kids how to own their mistakes without losing dignity.

For example, “I was wrong to raise my voice. I’ll work on being calmer” is a healthy apology. It acknowledges the mistake without groveling. Kids who see this learn that accountability builds trust.

Give them chores that matter

Chores aren’t just about cleaning up. They’re about teaching responsibility and contribution. When kids see that their work benefits the family, they learn they’re part of something bigger than themselves.

Instead of assigning meaningless tasks, give them chores that have a visible impact. Assembling a new table, feeding a pet, or helping to choose curtains for the home shows them that their opinion matters. This is a direct antidote to narcissistic thinking, which thrives on entitlement.

Teach them to spot manipulation

Kids who don’t learn to recognize manipulation may grow into adults who either use it or fall victim to it. Talk openly about what manipulation looks like: guilt trips, silent treatment, or exaggerated flattery.

You can point out examples in everyday life, like a TV character who uses guilt to get their way. This helps kids see the difference between healthy influence and unhealthy control. It’s one of the smartest ways to stop codependent narcissist traits from forming.

Balance independence with connection

Too much independence without connection can breed self-centeredness. Too many connections without independence can breed dependency. The balance is teaching kids to enjoy being with others while also being comfortable alone.

Encourage solo play as well as family activities. Let them spend time with friends, but also value family meals. This balance teaches them that relationships are important, but so is self-reliance.

Show them that feelings are not weakness

Kids who learn to bury feelings may grow into adults who seek control instead of vulnerability. Kids who learn to dramatize feelings could grow into adults who manipulate others. Rather, teach a child that feelings are natural and manageable.

Say things like, “It’s okay to feel sad, and it’s okay to talk about it.” This normalizes emotions without making them the center of attention.

Teach gratitude, not just saying “thank you”

Gratitude isn’t just polite words. It’s noticing the good in everyday life. Encourage kids to name what they’re thankful for: friends, meals, opportunities. Gratitude shifts focus away from entitlement and prevents codependent narcissistic traits from taking root.

You can make gratitude part of daily routines, like sharing one thing you’re thankful for at dinner. This simple practice builds perspective and humility.

Balance in parenting comes from the small, repeated choices that shape how kids see themselves and others. Over time, these everyday habits protect them from falling into the unhealthy patterns of a codependent narcissist and instead nurture resilience, humility, and emotional strength.

Signs You’re Helping Kids Avoid Codependent Narcissist Traits

Parents often wonder if their efforts are making a difference. There are clear signs that show kids are learning balance instead of leaning toward unhealthy patterns. When children express feelings openly without fear of being dismissed, take responsibility without constantly fishing for praise, and enjoy independence while still valuing connection, it shows they’re learning that relationships and self-reliance can coexist.

These signs may seem small, but they reflect deep lessons about identity, respect, and emotional health. They are evidence that your parenting practices are steering your child away from the traps of becoming a codependent narcissist and toward becoming an adult who is confident, compassionate, and balanced in how they relate to themselves and others.

Why Professional Counseling Helps

Parenting is full of trial and error, and no one gets it perfect. But being intentional about these practices helps kids grow into adults who are confident without being controlling, connected without being dependent.

If you’re worried about whether your child is showing signs of becoming a codependent narcissist, or if you want guidance on building healthier family patterns, professional counseling is a wise step. item.title: Understanding Autism in Women: 3 Support Strategies Beyond Medication
item.description:
For years, she thought she was simply “too sensitive.” Crowded stores felt exhausting. Bright lights were distracting. Conversations in groups felt overwhelming, and she often replayed them in her mind afterward, wondering if she had said the wrong thing. Many women spend years believing they are shy, anxious, or “too much,” only to discover later in life that Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may help explain experiences they have had since childhood.

Autism in women is often diagnosed at a much later age because the signs are either missed or diagnosed under different ailments (1). But when a woman does receive a diagnosis of ASD, there is promising research for treatments that do not rely as heavily on medication.

What Is Autism Spectrum Disorder?

ASD is a developmental, neurodivergent condition that involves significant challenges in communication and social interaction, as well as limitations in behavior patterns. This includes repetitive, highly limited or restricted interests, and inflexibility, among others. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria were updated by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022.

If you think you or a loved one may have ASD but have yet to be diagnosed, we recommend seeing a licensed therapist in one of our offices to discuss your concerns.

Why Autism in Women Gets Missed

There are several reasons a girl may be categorized as “normal” or as having a shy personality or possibly diagnosed with anxiety instead of autism when she’s growing up.

One reason is that anyone — female or male — who is naturally less expressive will not exhibit the expressive signs of another more overt personality who is struggling with social interaction. Another reason is that some of the research used to set the gold standard of autism measures was set using boys as the model, and girls present differently (1).

While a boy with autism may be flagged for an evaluation because he limits his toys to dinosaurs and stacks them repeatedly, a girl may not be flagged because she is playing with her dolls. However, what a teacher or parent might not notice is that within her pretend play, the girl is also exhibiting behavioral patterns that would signify the need for further assessment.

A girl may play by lining up the dolls and mimicking the same pretend story over and over. The reason the girl did not get assessed in the first place is that her play traits are more characteristic of her gender than the boy’s, and they are less noticeable.

Autism in women also gets missed because they learn to cope by masking their neurodivergent patterns of behavior and mimicking the behaviors they see of normalized social cues. This can be exhausting, and it often leads to burnout (2). For many women, masking becomes so automatic that they do not realize how much energy it requires until they begin experiencing chronic exhaustion or burnout. Many women do not seek treatment until they recognize the signs of burnout and wonder what could be causing their extreme responses to what appear to be everyday social interactions.

What Might Autism in Women Look Like?

Women with autism have similar interests to any woman, but some of the neurodivergences can include:

● Preferring one-on-one discussions instead of group discussions
● Sensory avoidance and sensitivity to light or sound
● Internalizing shutdowns so they appear to be zoning out, but in actuality, they are overwhelmed by external stimuli
● Practicing scripts to mimic the social norms that are expected
● Adopting personas to become like what they think they should be, e.g., an organized student or a helpful co-worker
● Stemming behaviors that aren’t as overt, such as hair twirling, cuticle picking, or quiet humming
● Misunderstanding conflicts, particularly in relationships or friendships
● Inability to maintain long-term friendships due to frustration, inflexibility, or limited interests

While every person is different, autism in women can also appear differently because there are levels of autism. These are some of the characteristics that might help you or someone you love find something relatable and a reason to reach out.

Treatments for Autism in Women Beyond Medicine

While medicines can provide relief to specific symptoms, this article maintains that a licensed counselor will work with a woman to determine those. It is important not to self-diagnose. Some women will have other conditions alongside ASD, and it is essential to understand their entire mental health portfolio to manage all conditions together.

Recent research suggests that a promising discovery could be beneficial, particularly for women (3) who struggle with sensory challenges related to autism. Using VR technology, one small study noted that women were better able to self-regulate when they were overstimulated. The technology allowed them to choose their own room filled with silence, and it did not matter what their physical location was.

This game-changer could be pivotal in helping anyone with autism, particularly in areas where moving locations is not an option, such as traveling through airports or in shopping malls. The research and prototype are still in their early stages, but the findings are promising.

Other treatments include resource-based support, such as guiding adolescents into adulthood by helping them with life skills and communication. An Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) support can help adolescents transition through coaching that’s targeted to their specific needs.

The ABA might include breaking down large skill sets into smaller chunks for practical problem-solving. Practical examples are using ABA to ensure you are getting on the right bus at the end of your shift, or how to answer questions appropriately in a job interview.

Self-assessment and reflection tools also help autistic adults as they learn how to identify their own skill gaps. Then, they can recognize what guidance could be helpful as they seek treatment from a therapist. Reflecting on how they feel in relationships, friendships, or the workplace may help reveal a particular challenge with interpersonal communication.

On the other hand, a guided tool geared toward women with autism may ask about self-care habits, such as sleep, hobbies, and routines. These questions can provide clues related to a need for more attention to broadening interests or expanding routines.

Vocation and social support are also shown to be effective. Especially for autism in women, you or your loved one may have wondered why a specific line of work has been so challenging, and the diagnosis may shed some light on it.

With vocational support and the Americans with Disabilities Act, several companies are designing inclusive workspaces, programs, and workplace roles that enable a person diagnosed with ASD to thrive. Social support may include one-on-one peer feedback or group therapy, both guided by licensed therapists.

Research on Autism in Women

While the research on autism in women is still emerging, the future of support, treatment, and vitality is strong. Several universities have developed programs of study for adult learners with autism, recognizing the need for further advancement.

One recent study showed that clinicians need to keep autism on their radar when women seek treatment for other conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, burnout, and ADHD. Some women may have comorbidities or have been misdiagnosed at the time they initially sought treatment.

Next Steps

If you suspect that you or another adult woman you know has autism, there are a few ways you can help. Depending on the nature of your relationship, you can consider the following:

· When was the most recent appointment with her primary care physician?
· What other challenges are present?
· What are some of the past obstacles socially, academically, and interpersonally?

After that, or if you are the person you suspect may be autistic, you can contact a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist who specializes in ASD. Our offices are staffed with therapists who have the appropriate training and experience to help you on your journey to thriving and well-being.

One thing to keep in mind is that there is not one test or assessment that clinicians use to decide if you have autism. Instead, the diagnosis will be based on a variety of questionnaires, your medical and health history, and you will likely need multiple appointments. But the important part is that you will have access to support once you are diagnosed — whether you have autism or not.

Take the first step and reach out for an initial evaluation. In the meantime, you can read articles about autism spectrum disorder and watch videos of other adults who were diagnosed later in life. It may encourage you to hear about their stories, so you will be informed, educated, and motivated for the path ahead.

Autism in women is often more complex to assess than in men, especially during childhood and adolescence. If you relate to anything you’ve read here, it is wise to seek an expert opinion. Contact an office near you today.

2. Gonçalves Garcia, S., da Silveira Simões-Pires, C., Acosta Brum, J., & Centurion Cabral, J. (2026). Taking off the mask: Investigating autism diagnosis and camouflaging in adult women. Autism in Adulthood, 8(4), 677-686.
3. Leonardi, S., Di Cara, M., Giliberto, S., Piccolo, A., De Domenico, C., Leonardi, G., … & Cucinotta, F. (2025). The use of multisensory environments in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism, 29(8), 1921-1938.Photos:

item.title: Understanding and Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma
item.description:
Can we ever truly escape the past? Sometimes it can feel as though the past repeats itself, and its chains have us in an iron grip we cannot release ourselves from.

It can be daunting to look at your own past and see the ways it reaches into your present. Wounds from the past, such as intergenerational trauma, can influence your day-to-day patterns and behavior. The good news is that the future is an open vista, and lasting healing is a real possibility.

Intergenerational Trauma: What Is It?

When we think about trauma, we often think about painful or distressing experiences that happen directly to us. Intergenerational trauma, however, refers to the ways the effects of trauma can continue beyond the generation that originally experienced it. Unresolved emotional wounds, learned beliefs, unhealthy coping strategies, relationship patterns, and responses to fear or stress can influence children and later generations, even when they did not experience the original traumatic event themselves.

Intergenerational trauma can occur within families or entire communities and may be passed down in subtle as well as more obvious ways. Over time, these patterns can affect a person’s emotional well-being, relationships, behaviors, and even how they understand themselves and the world around them.

People experiencing intergenerational trauma may struggle with forming healthy relationships, unexplained depression or anxiety, patterns of self-sabotage or fear, or a sense of carrying a burden they struggle to name. These effects can occur in the present even when the original painful or traumatic events happened decades or generations before.

Some Examples of Intergenerational Trauma in Scripture

While the term ‘intergenerational trauma’ is something that has gained currency in recent decades, that does not mean that the reality it names is new. Scripture is quite candid about how sin has consequences; our brokenness and the brokenness of others that we endure, and experience all have consequences, and these can ripple through generations.

Two examples of this can help us. One is to consider the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which we read about from Genesis 12 until the end of the book. In story after story, there are repeated patterns of deeply damaging favoritism, selfishness, and deception, which cause ongoing conflict and shape the dynamics in the family across generations. In Jacob’s story, in particular, the threat of violence looms as he interacts with his brother Esau and his uncle, Laban.

Another example is David, a great king, warrior, and a man with many moral failings. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging to have her husband killed, the Lord warned David that his actions would have lasting consequences in his own family (2 Samuel 11-12). David’s own son sexually assaulted his half-sister, and David did nothing about it. As a result, his family experienced even more violence and betrayal through revenge and a violent civil war.

The cycles of violence, betrayal, deception, and more that affected these families are tied to longstanding patterns of behavior that are rooted even further in the past. While this is true, Scripture also tells us that there is hope in the Lord to break such cycles.

There is the possibility of redemption, restoration, and a brand-new story for those who seek Him and pursue the new life that is possible in Him (Romans 8; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Causes and Triggers of Intergenerational Trauma

From what is known, intergenerational trauma has its roots in a traumatic experience a person, family, or community has. A significant event, unresolved pain, or prolonged suffering can be at the root of what goes on to become intergenerational trauma. These events could include abuse, abandonment or loss, poverty, war, forced migration, and familial patterns of violence or addiction.

These various events and experiences operate on several levels. Some of them, like experiences of war, genocide, or forced migration and displacement, are collective events that scar entire communities. Facing systemic oppression and stress from poverty and discrimination can also affect a community that is the target of such measures. There are also family dysfunctions, such as abuse, addiction, neglect, or abandonment, that can become normalized over time in a family unit.

Future generations within a community or family may not experience the original traumatic event. Still, they may inherit emotional and behavioral patterns that were formed as a response to the pain. These patterns would include anxious attachment, aggression, or deep mistrust.

Intergenerational trauma and its effects may become more noticeable during times of stress or transition. These experiences can activate learned emotional and behavioral patterns, attachment wounds, and stress responses that have been shaped by family experiences across generations.

For example, getting married or becoming a parent can trigger unresolved attachment wounds from one’s childhood or resurface old family patterns.

Other situations that may trigger this trauma include conflict situations and situations of loss and injustice that mirror those of past generations. Such conflict situations may trigger inherited anger or fears. Witnessing violence in one’s community or going through financial hardship can also activate a heightened stress response that affects one’s physical and mental well-being.

Some Signs of Intergenerational Trauma to Look Out for

Intergenerational trauma can manifest in various ways. Often, it escapes detection because it can appear as normal, and just the way your family or community does things. To pick up on how certain patterns are rooted in trauma and anything but ‘normal’ requires close examination and the willingness to make changes toward a healthier outlook. Some signs to look out for include the following:

Hypervigilance This is when you are constantly on edge, and you feel unsafe even in safe spaces.

Unhealthy relationship patterns This includes patterns of shame, denial, secrecy, mistrust, and recurring patterns of codependency.

Relational breakdown Patterns of repeated relational breakdowns across generations within the family may also point to intergenerational trauma.

Emotional problems Issues with regulating moods and emotions, persistent anxiety, depression, or emotional numbness may suggest intergenerational trauma. Also, having emotional overreactions to seemingly unrelated events could be the result of reacting to past traumas.

Inherited beliefs Carrying certain unstated or unconscious beliefs that shape your self-understanding could be a sign of intergenerational trauma. These beliefs could include feeling you are not worthy or that the world is a dangerous place. Persistent feelings of guilt or worthlessness without a clear cause may suggest intergenerational trauma.

Physical symptoms These would include insomnia, chronic pain, or stress-related conditions like heart disease.

A list of possible symptoms is a first step to help you identify what you or a loved one may be experiencing. However, various physical, emotional, and mental health challenges carry similar symptoms, and that is why it’s important to see a health professional. They can help you eliminate possible causes so that you can identify the root cause and address it.

Finding Healing from Intergenerational Trauma

This article started by posing a question – can we ever truly escape the past? Your past is your past, and you cannot change it. However, there is always hope for your future to look different, and to lessen the hold of the past on the here and now. There is freedom in Christ (Galatians 5:1), and with help, you can confront the past to step into a new chapter for you and your loved ones.

“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” John 8:36 ESV

The path to hope and a new future may include the following:

Acknowledge the pain Healing comes when you identify that there is a problem, a set of patterns of behaviors that are undermining the fullness of life the Lord intends for you. Reflect on your family history, naming the patterns there and recognizing how they have shaped you.

Seek the Lord’s healing You can do this through prayer, reading Scripture, and allowing Him to bring light into the dark spaces in your life. Lament is a powerful way to express your pain to the Lord, and speaking unspoken grief to the Lord in the pattern of the lament Psalms can help you find release.

Forgive and let go Forgiveness does not excuse harm; it helps you break the cycle of resentment and harm as you release the grip of the past on who you are and will be.

Set new patterns Make intentional choices empowered by God’s Spirit and grace to create new family traditions, communicate in a different style, and so on.

Seek counseling A trained Christian counselor can help you identify and unpack the deep wounds and trauma, break harmful patterns of thinking and behavior, and begin building healthier responses to everyday life.

Through faith-based counseling alongside trauma-informed therapies such as internal family systems or cognitive behavioral therapy, your counselor can help you process these deep wounds in a safe environment.

Healing the wounds of the past can start with you today. Reach out to our office or contact our reception team to connect with a counselor who can walk with you on your journey toward healing and wholeness.

item.title: Caring for Others Without Losing Yourself: The Importance of Caregiver Support
item.description:
There is one myth I believe many caregivers unknowingly live by. It is the belief that caring for someone else requires you to lose yourself. At first, this does not seem true. Most caregivers never wake up one morning deciding to abandon their own life. It happens little by little. It happens through responsibility. It happens through love. It happens through necessity. It happened because you took vows, and you are choosing to honor them at all costs.

Caregiving is unique because many people never choose it. It chooses them. One phone call changed everything. A stroke changes everything. It did for me. A diagnosis changes everything. It was for my mom. An accident changes everything. It does for many. Suddenly, the life you knew becomes the life you used to have.

You are no longer simply a husband, a wife, a daughter, a son. You become a caregiver; a grieving, at times confused, overwhelmed, resentful, hurt caregiver. While everyone is watching the person who is sick, few people are watching the one providing the care.

People pity caregivers, but do not support caregivers or the act of caregiving. Due to this, as one who cares for others, it is important to have key things in place to ensure you have a more pleasant experience while staying present.

Caregiving rarely begins with a choice

Most people prepare for careers. They prepare for marriage. They prepare to become parents. Few prepare to become caregivers. But I think there is room for us to start. This is a thought we will explore another time.

For those coming face to face with aging parents, you discover that one doctor’s appointment is turning into several. Hospital visits are becoming too frequent, therefore, normal. Medication schedules are replacing personal routines. Home modifications are now necessary. As the calendar slowly fills with appointments that belong to your mom or dad.

Before long, you have begun measuring each day by the needs of another person. Not to mention that you are not the one who is familiar with the doctors, and now your name is listed on official medical paperwork. You are caregiving, not just being a good son or daughter, husband or wife, friend or neighbor.

This shift happened

When someone you love or care about becomes ill, their health becomes the priority, as it should. Their recovery deserves attention. Their safety deserves protection. Their life deserves every reasonable effort. The challenge is that while their needs move to the front, yours slowly move to the back. Not because you no longer matter.

Because there never seems to be enough room for both. Why? Because family and friends who get thrust into caregiving begin giving out of necessity and panic while the knowledge of needed caregiving organization and balance is unknown to them. A caregiver in this situation does not mean to lose themselves; it just happened.

When The Sick Become the Center

Here is something that you need to know: illness naturally changes the focus of a family. Conversations become centered around symptoms. Decisions become centered around treatments. Finances become centered around medical expenses. Time becomes centered around recovery. Everything else begins to pale in comparison. Nothing seems to be more urgent. Your hobbies get put on hold. Your friendship gets put on pause. Your dreams get halted.

The caregiver often convinces themselves this is only temporary. Yet months become years. Seasons continue to change while the caregiver remains standing in the same place emotionally. This is where losing yourself quietly begins. Not through one major decision. Through thousands of small ones.

My small decisions began with seeing the need in me to bathe daily. It seemed as though when I bathed my husband, that was the most important. My needs were not. At the time of his stroke, we lived in a three-story townhome. We did not go outside for over four months. He was in prison with the punishment of the stroke, so was I.

However, I did not understand until later that he did not need me to live as if I were sick too. He needed to see me live so he could be inspired to get back to living. He wanted to see me beautified as his wife.

The Slow Disappearance of The Caregiver

This is how you know you have lost yourself as a caregiver. Losing yourself is rarely dramatic; it is more often subtle.

  • You stop asking yourself what you need.
  • You stop noticing your own exhaustion.
  • You stop celebrating your own accomplishments.
  • You stop making plans that include your own future.
  • Eventually someone asks how you are doing. Your first response is to talk about the person you care for. You no longer know how to answer the question for yourself.
  • You begin introducing yourself by someone else’s condition instead of your own life.

Watch out for this mislabeling of yourself as a caregiver. Identity is one of the first things to be disrupted as a caregiver.

  • You become the wife of the stroke survivor.
  • The husband of the spouse with cancer.
  • The daughter caring for her aging mother.
  • The son caring for his father.

These descriptions are true. They simply should not become your entire identity. There is honor in caring for others, and I do not want that to go unsaid here. Nevertheless, remember that caring for others requires you to remain able to do so.

This means that emotionally, mentally, and physically, it would be great for you to be in a stable place so that you can help from that same place. A caregiver that is inwardly secure and happy can truly go the distance in care for an individual in a pleasant and effective way. Being a caregiver is one thing; how you give care is another.

What I Wish I Had Known

As a caregiver what I wished I had known is what were some of the key tips that I needed to ensure that it was easier and how to do what was expected of me. I learned how to bathe my husband the hard way. I dressed him the hard way. I helped him use the bathroom the hard way. I fed him the hard way.

Everything I did, I will add “the hard way” because I did not know “how” to do it for a person who was disabled. This would have allowed me to save time and energy which would have helped me not to lose myself so easily in “tying” what was not the best for his condition at the time. Time and method are important.

I mentioned earlier about organization. This tags time and method for me. As a caregiver you won’t be able to get away from the tasks of what is required doctors’ visits, medication runs etc. But how you organize them is up to you. You can use delivery of medication or easier pick-up methods.

Additionally, make sure you have the medication by going to the most convenient pharmacy for you as the caregiver, not the patient. It is also wise to ensure that appointments are synced on the same day as much as possible or sprinkled throughout the week with your errands so that you and the patient are getting what you need.

Organize locations, activities, grocery trips, and leisure outings to ensure everyone gets what they need. As a caregiver, don’t forget our appointments and do not forget to schedule downtime or naps to recharge. You can do that.

Also, do not forget to schedule time to enjoy the relationship with the person and not to emphasize the duty to the person. The relationship is key to nurture while caring for them physically. I wish I had known to protect them a bit more with walks in the park, talks about emotional needs, not just physical or medical, and moments of meaningful physical touch. This includes hugs, hand-holding, kisses, etc.

The person receiving care deserves your best. Your best becomes much more difficult to give when you have nothing remaining inside yourself. Do it for them. Do it for you. Do it for the relationship.

item.title: How to Define OCD: Three Areas That Are Helped By Counseling
item.description:
The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders defines obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) as:

“…the presence of obsessions and /or compulsions. Obsessions are recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, whereas compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts that an individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly” – American Psychiatric Association, 2022

Although concise, this definition can be made more understandable by breaking down different elements of this disorder. The two main components of this disorder are obsessions and compulsions.

Obsessions/Intrusive Thoughts

Obsessions are consistent thoughts, impulsive feelings or mental pictures that take place repeatedly in one’s mind. They take place without the person causing them and without the person wanting them to be there; this is where the term intrusive comes from. The thought, image, or urge intrudes on a person.

There are all sorts of obsessions that one might have, and they are as varied as people are. One person might experience an obsession as an intrusive thought that they have committed a sin, but that is only the beginning for someone with OCD. The thought of possibly committing a sin won’t leave their mind, and they find themself thinking about it over and over again, even when they don’t want to. This category would be called religious OCD or scrupulosity.

Another example of an obsession might be someone who feels an intrusive impulse (urge) to harm someone in some way and they are horrified by the realization. They continue to experience it over and over again, feeling more horror and more shame with each experience of it. This category is called harm OCD.

Yet another example might be someone who has intrusive mental images of sexual acts. This person does not want these images and is disgusted and horrified by them but cannot seem to get them out of their head. This would fall under the category of sexual OCD.

Because clinicians have noticed patterns among those who are diagnosed with OCD, obsessions have been grouped into particular categories, such as the ones used in the examples above. Other categories include but are not limited to hoarding/saving, symmetry/order, contamination, somatic (having to do with the body), and relationships.

Compulsions

It is often the case that both obsessions and compulsions are present in an individual who is diagnosed with OCD; however, only one of these needs to be present to meet the criteria for an OCD diagnosis.

The other component to a diagnosis of OCD is compulsions. Compulsions are physical or mental actions repeated over and over. These actions are characterized by an urge to complete them or by a particular and precise way of completing them. Compulsions are sometimes called “safety behaviors.” They are called this because one forms a belief that if they complete the behavior, they will be or feel safe.

For example, think of someone who has a contamination obsession. This person might obsess about the spread of germs. Their compulsion might be to clean everything that might have come in contact with germs. The compulsion might make them feel “safe” from germs, but only temporarily.

The trouble is that as the person uses the compulsion (cleaning) to temporarily feel safe, they are inadvertently training their mind that cleaning must happen to relieve the fear of germs spreading. The more one completes the compulsion, the stronger their belief that the compulsion will keep them safe from spreading germs.

You may see where this is going. The compulsions require more and more from the sufferer because it is not possible to be safe from all germs, and somewhere in their mind, they are aware of that. This awareness drives them to continue to try to fix the problem of germs being a danger. The solution to this is not to be or feel entirely safe from the effects of germs, as this is impossible. However, the OCD sufferer believes that this is the solution.

The Goal of OCD Treatment

In reality, the solution to symptoms of OCD is to build up the capacity to tolerate the discomfort and fear that comes with the thought of germs. The more this tolerance is built up, the less the compulsion will feel needed.

The same is true for any category of OCD: the OCD sufferer has convinced himself that the compulsion brings safety, but the reality is that it does not bring safety but demands continued engagement in the compulsions and mounting fear that drives the obsession. There are specific fears behind every obsession, and the goal for treatment of OCD is to build up a tolerance and a capacity to live with those fears.

Ways That Counseling Can Help

Sharing Obsessions and Intrusive Thoughts

Many people with OCD find the intrusive thoughts, obsessions, and compulsions they experience as frightening or shameful. This often leads to suffering in silence and fear, without knowing these are symptoms of OCD and without knowing that there are people who can offer help and support.

In particular, those who suffer from harm and sexual OCD symptoms often believe that they are bad people for having these unwanted and intrusive thoughts or compulsions. The word intrusive means that the thought is unwanted, uninvited, and unexpected. As you may be able to imagine, having sexual images suddenly come into your mind or unexpectedly thinking about harming another person would be quite disturbing!

This is common in those who suffer from OCD. The truth is that all people experience thoughts that are unwanted. Those who do not have OCD move past these thoughts without forming any judgments about themselves or the thoughts. Those with OCD have thoughts about these thoughts, which often lead to compulsions to get rid of these disturbances.

Meeting with a counselor and sharing these thoughts, obsessions, or compulsions with them can offer great relief from shame. Counseling can offer a place where someone can share these things that disturb them, and they will not be met with judgment but with compassion and help.

This is an important step for those who suffer from OCD. Being able to share this part of their life with another person who does not believe that they are “bad” for any of these things can bring a profound sense of relief and a starting point for continued treatment of OCD.

Tolerating Discomfort and Fear with Support

Once a person has been able to share these disturbing obsessions and compulsions with a caring counselor who does not respond with judgment, support and treatment can be discussed. The most common and efficacious treatment for OCD is called Exposure Response Prevention (ERP).

The first step is exposing the person to the fear behind the obsession. There are many ways to do this. Some people can use real-world exposures, and some can use imagining different scenarios as an exposure. This is done in the presence of a counselor, and the individual will share their emotional experience with the counselor.

It is important to note that the process of exposure causes great anxiety and fear to emerge in the individual. The purpose of this is to reform the brain processes to allow the person to not engage in a compulsion when they normally would and to teach themself that they do have the ability to tolerate the fear and discomfort they are attempting to avoid.

Response prevention involves the individual refraining from engaging in the compulsion or safety behavior, whatever that might look like. The point of refraining from the safety behavior is to train the brain and body to tolerate the discomfort of the fear or anxiety experienced when not engaging in the compulsion.

Eventually, the intensity of discomfort will subside, and the exposure will be over. This can be an overwhelming and scary experience, and this is why it is important to do it with a trained and caring counselor. The goal is for the individual to grow skilled at doing this so that they can practice it outside of their treatment with a counselor and eventually be able to do it on their own.

Identifying Unhelpful Thinking Patterns

An important part of treatment for OCD is identifying different thinking patterns that are not helpful. All of us experience what we might call automatic thoughts. These are generally based on different beliefs that we have about the world or ourselves.

For example, one person might experience an urge to floor the gas pedal as they are stopped in rush hour traffic. An automatic thought from someone who does not suffer from OCD might be “Wow, that’s a weird urge to have” or “That’s kind of funny that urge just showed up in my mind.” Someone who suffers from OCD might have the thought of “I’m a terrible person who cannot be trusted to operate a vehicle!”

The automatic thought of the person who suffers from OCD could bring up feelings of guilt, fear, shame, etc. If one can identify this automatic thought, one can then decide if they truly believe that thought. More often than not, these automatic thoughts contain errors in logic.

In this example, one of the errors in logic might be that the person is confusing feelings with facts. The person feels terrible for having that image come into their head, but that doesn’t mean that they are terrible for having that image come into their head. Slowly, with time and support from a trained counselor, these automatic thoughts can be identified and examined for alignment with the truth.

In summary, obsessions and/or compulsions are the components that are the diagnostic makeup of obsessive-compulsive disorder. As with all mental disorders, for one to be diagnosed, the symptoms must cause significant difficulty in functioning. In other words, the mere presence of obsessions or compulsions in one’s life does not mean that one meets the criteria for an OCD diagnosis. It is when it gets in the way of functioning that it becomes a mental disorder.

There are three significant ways that counseling can help one who suffers from OCD: sharing obsessions, intrusive thoughts, or compulsions with a non-judgmental and skilled counselor; engaging in ERP treatment; and learning to identify and slowly change unhelpful thought patterns.

There are many other ways that counseling can help those who suffer from OCD; this list is not exhaustive. Those with OCD need not suffer in silence nor continue to be bound by OCD; there is hope and people who want to support you in healing!

item.title: Overwhelming Anxiety: Why the Anxious Mind Replays the Past
item.description:
Anxiety is multifaceted, complex, and yes, a relentless machine. If you live with overwhelming anxiety, you know that it often feels more powerful than you. Not only does it give you racing thoughts, tight muscles, and the need for hypervigilance, but it is also more annoying than the worst playground bully.

Anxiety, the aggressive historian that it is, has the exhausting superpower of dragging you back in time. Overwhelming anxiety feels like it is forcing you to sit in a theater of your own making and watch replays of your most painful and embarrassing moments.

Why does overwhelming anxiety dwell in the past?

Someone without anxiety might look to the past for the sake of nostalgia or maybe even to look for meaning or lessons in their most painful moments. The anxious brain, however, relentlessly scans history for a different reason. It loops through painful memories and uncertain moments because it’s terrified of the future.

Deep down, overwhelming anxiety operates on a core belief. It fully believes that if it can figure out exactly what went wrong in past painful experiences, it can keep those and other bad things from happening in the future.

Anxiety is an authoritarian that forces you into the role of a detective who’s tasked with examining a crime scene. You must analyze data, searching for hidden clues you missed or rewriting conversation scripts as if this new dialogue can also rewrite history.

This is called rumination and is vastly different from healthy self-analysis or reflection on the past. While acknowledging a mistake and learning from a lesson is healthy, an anxious mind refuses to move on from it, even after the lesson is learned.

On a conscious level, you might recognize that no amount of dwelling can edit an already existing past or change an outcome. Subconsciously, the anxious brain treats these memories as a present or future threat that must be dealt with.

How Your Body Handles Overwhelming Anxiety

As if ruminating thoughts aren’t enough of a debt to pay for past missteps or pain, the anxious mind drags the body into the punishment, too. When a memory surfaces, it’s no longer just a historical record, but your body views it as a physical threat. Your stomach might tighten as your jaw clenches. Your heart rate may increase as your body sensations experience the past as if it is playing out again in real time.

Unfortunately, the human body can’t always distinguish between an emotionally charged memory from the past and an authentic present threat. While your rational brain may know that the embarrassing conversation ended long ago or the aggressive confrontation is already over, the nervous system still responds as if the danger is imminent.

God of the Past and the Future

When the anxious mind fixates on the past, it almost always does so through a lens of harsh accusation and criticism. The instant replays it insists you view aren’t objective but are heavily edited to show your flaws and perceived inadequacies.

The Enemy loves to use the anxious mind’s natural tendency toward rumination to convince you that your current worth is directly linked to your past mistakes and negative circumstances.

Thankfully, God is more powerful than Satan. He is more powerful than you or your anxiety, too. In Isaiah 43, God speaks directly to the people of Israel during a period of exile. They were a people who felt burdened by their history, much like you might. “Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it?” (Isaiah 43:18-19, NIV)

Notice that God doesn’t tell them “Don’t look back,” or that they should ignore their past trauma entirely. Instead, He is telling them not to dwell there. And then He asks them a question. Maybe this is the question He is asking you. He asks if they have perceived the new thing that He’s doing in their lives.

When you get so wrapped up in deciphering and rescripting the past, you often lose sight of the goodness of God. If you make that memory the idol in which you are fixated, you might miss the new thing that God is doing as a result of that past trauma or mistake.

Forgiveness and Anxiety

Was your past painful? Did you make mistakes? Even if the answer is yes to this and all the other accusatory questions your brain asks you, it doesn’t matter in God’s eyes.

While your anxious brain might want you to pay penance for your past, God wants you to live abundantly. He forgives your mistakes, even when you can’t forgive yourself. Numerous Scriptures reinforce the concept of God’s forgiveness and redemption. Psalm 103 says, “…as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” (Psalm 103:12, NIV)

When your anxious brain replays your past through a lens of condemnation or shame, you can remind yourself of that Scripture. Once you’ve asked God to forgive you through Jesus Christ, He removes your sins and casts them into an infinite, unreachable place. And you have no business trying to drag those memories back into the present.

God Is Doing a New Thing

God’s forgiveness is a life-giving reality, but His love doesn’t stop there. When you’re a child of God, even your past can’t haunt you forever. Will you have consequences for your actions? Yes, of course, there are natural consequences. God is also able to intervene and protect you from your own missteps and from those who might have hurt you in the past.

“And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose.” (Romans 8:28, NIV) The beauty of this verse is that it doesn’t try to gaslight you into believing that everything is good, but it shows you that those painful situations that you keep replaying can be used to build something purposeful in God’s Hands.

In Genesis, Joseph says to his brothers, “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.” (Genesis 50:20, NIV) Joseph could have allowed the pain of his brothers’ betrayal to define him or keep him stuck in the past.

Joseph acknowledges the reality that his brothers intended to harm him by selling him into slavery. Yet he recognized that God’s supreme authority and unrelenting love for him took those ill intentions and turned them into massive blessings.

He can do that for you, too. He can take your past traumas, awkward conversations, and all those mistakes you’ve been replaying. They don’t have to continue to condemn or define you. God wants you to break free from those ties that bind you to the past trauma.

Breaking Free

While God can instantly deliver you from anxiety, sometimes healing is a process. If your brain is caught in a loop of memories and rumination, a Christian counselor can help you break free from the relentlessness.

Therapy provides the opportunity to dig into your past to determine where your anxiety comes from. A therapist can help you understand your options for dealing with past trauma, learned responses, and biological predispositions.

Through a variety of techniques, a therapist can help you redirect those automatic replays the moment they start. They can help you learn how to challenge the lies that your brain is telling you and help you realize that analyzing and replaying a situation does not offer you protection.

If you or a loved one feels exhausted from constantly reliving the past, reach out to our office today. Let us help you process your past so it doesn’t negatively impact your future.

item.title: Understanding and Finding Help for Nighttime Anxiety from a Faith-Based Perspective
item.description:
To the outside eye, the scene looks tranquil. The lights are out, and the fan provides a steady harmony and the occasional soft breeze. There are no loud neighbors or barking dogs. In fact, there’s nothing that could derail the perfect night’s rest. Nothing except nighttime anxiety.

What Is Nighttime Anxiety?

Nighttime anxiety is the nervousness, worry, or panic that occurs just before bed or late in the evening. It’s not a distinct or separate medical diagnosis, but rather a common manifestation of generalized anxiety or stress that peaks when the distractions of the day fade away.

While daytime anxiety is often tied to immediate tasks and interactions, nighttime anxiety tends to be more introspective. It frequently causes you to focus on existential worries or get stuck replaying the day’s troubles, even if they are minor.

What Nighttime Anxiety Feels Like

Nighttime anxiety behaves the same as it does during the day but can be more obvious or intense because of several factors. Some of these are emotional or mentally internal while others are physical.

There are the characteristic racing thoughts and possibly a racing heart. There’s likely physical tension as muscles stiffen and breathing becomes irregular. It is common to feel dread or panic that feels overwhelming, too. The intensity of anxiety can vary from person to person. While some experience a sense of uneasiness, some people with more severe cases experience nocturnal panic attacks that can wake them from sleep.

It’s a feeling that’s hard to explain unless you’ve gone through it. And while most people can identify with feelings of anxiety, clinical anxiety disorders are different than normal, everyday stress. Anxiety at night can be more intense and recurring. It can feel terrifying and crippling when anxiety occurs at night.

Why Does it Happen at Night?

For many people, anxiety becomes more noticeable at night, simply because there are fewer distractions than during the day. During the daytime hours, there are many other distractions to draw your interest, which helps to quiet the voice of anxiety.

There are conversations to have, errands to run, work to be finished, and people to take care of. In these busiest of moments, the mind stays occupied by all the distractions. But when the world slows down, unresolved issues and familiar anxious thoughts can crawl their way back to the surface. While the silence of the night should be a source of comfort, for some people with anxiety disorders, this quietness can quickly turn into toxic overthinking and anxiety.

Anxiety triggers vary. For some people, conversations that didn’t land as well as intended start playing in a loop. Those embarrassing moments get magnified. For others, worries of the future suddenly become realistic outcomes rather than far-fetched possibilities. You might worry about your health, your loved ones, finances, parenting, or even the purpose of life, before you even get the alarm set for the next morning.

Fatigue and Nighttime Anxiety

Fatigue also plays a role in how you respond to anxiety. After a full day of work, stress, and responsibilities, your body and your mind can feel exhausted. This deep state of fatigue weakens your ability to reason calmly or to cope effectively with the problems your anxious brain presents to you.

Fewer Distractions

For some people, nighttime anxiety digs a little deeper into insecurities and deep-seated fears. Maybe the struggle of being alone or fear of a terminal illness are the most terrifying triggers you can imagine. These worries are not necessarily triggered by a nighttime routine, although that is sometimes a factor, but are present constantly.

Things like this might be more manageable during the day, when you have to be calm for others. However, these deeply rooted fears surface with a vengeance in the quiet of the night.

Anxiety Loves Isolation

Because anxiety loves isolation, it often does its most sinister work in the dark cover of night. When you are with others, there is often a social pressure to act calm. Sometimes, the act of appearing calm can actually help keep your anxiety in check temporarily.

As you pretend to be at peace, your body can be triggered to react peacefully. While pretending to be calm during the day might temporarily keep anxiety at bay, suppressing it all day often leaves you emotionally exhausted by bedtime.

Another reason anxiety feels more intense at night is that if it strikes during the day, you can sometimes quiet its voice immediately by talking with a trusted person. Even if you’re not with a person you feel comfortable talking to about your biggest fears, the simple act of being around others (assuming they are not part of what is causing the anxiety) can help calm anxious feelings because humans were created for community and social interaction.

At night, you are often alone. This can make it difficult to find support when you struggle with nighttime anxiety.

Habitual Triggers

One attribute of anxiety that is particularly pronounced in people who also have Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is the nighttime routine. If you have a set nighttime routine, you might be inadvertently contributing to your nighttime anxiety.

That’s not to say that you shouldn’t have a routine. In fact, routines can be part of a healthy and calming sleep. But the wrong type of routine can cause nighttime anxiety. If you are in the habit of scrolling through social media just before bed, you could be feeding your anxiety with more things to hyperfocus on, like triggering news stories or a new person to compare yourself to.

Maybe some part of your nighttime routine has become associated with a deep-seated worry. For example, your routine of checking and rechecking your door lock is a response to a prior burglary. While checking to make sure the house is secure is common sense, doing it repeatedly at night might be keeping the trauma of the burglary at the forefront of your mind when you’re at your most vulnerable.

What To Do About Nighttime Anxiety

Sleep is a vital part of overall health. If anxiety is preventing you from getting a good night’s rest, here are some ideas on how to calm those nighttime fears.

Change Your Routine

If your bedtime routine is triggering anxious thoughts, change it. Even a routine that looks healthy on the exterior and one that has served you well before might trigger anxiety now.

Sometimes routines become unintentionally tied to fear or stress. Your brain begins associating certain activities, sounds, or even certain times of night with anxiety itself. If that has been happening, introducing new and calming habits can help break that connection.

Be Responsible, Not Obsessive

If your habit of checking to make sure the house is secure reminds you of a traumatic experience, then find a safe workaround. If possible, pass the responsibility of checking door locks and other safety issues off on another responsible adult in the home. Or perform this routine earlier in the night, so it isn’t directly associated with your bedtime behavior.

Reassociate Bed with Joy

Anxious brains are often creative brains. When a creative brain suddenly has no external stimuli to focus on, it gets bored. Anxiety sometimes strikes through that vulnerability and forces you to turn inward. If you associate bedtime with worry and fear, it can become a habit that’s difficult to break. But you can break it when you flip the script on your anxiety.

Try going to bed a little bit earlier and indulge in an activity you will look forward to. Keep a good book on your nightstand and allow yourself a fifteen-minute window before bed to enjoy it, for example. Whatever brings you joy, whether that’s photos of loved ones, a new sudoku book, or even a beloved pet, make it part of your bedtime routine.

Invite God

Inviting the Prince of Peace into your night will not only usher in the sweet peace of the Holy Spirit but remind you of the goodness of God. Say a simple prayer, have an honest conversation with your Creator, read Scriptures, or play worship music softly in the background. Anything you can do to infuse God into your nightly routine is bound to bring comfort.

Therapy Can Help Nighttime Anxiety

There is something at the heart of your nighttime anxiety, even if the cause is unclear. Finding the root cause can help you better understand not only what your anxiety is doing but why it is showing up at night. Therapy can provide a structured place for you to explore those patterns with someone who’s trained to help you without judgment.

If you’re struggling with nighttime anxiety, call us today to make an appointment. Together with your trained counselor, you can start to reclaim your night and finally get peaceful sleep.

item.title: When You’re Getting Older and Still Haven’t Found Love
item.description:
Most of the love stories in Hollywood suggest that life doesn’t truly begin until you find the one. We are conditioned to believe that if we just wait long enough or stay attractive enough and thin enough, our own happily ever after will eventually arrive.

But when you’re sitting solo while your younger friends or relatives celebrate anniversaries or the birth of their children, that happily-ever-after narrative starts to feel less like a promise and more like a sucker punch. It can leave you feeling left out or unworthy. It can make you feel envious of people who are just living out their lives, unaware of your secret longing and hurt.

Dealing with your aloneness when you’ve asked God for a partner.

Grow where you’re planted

This isn’t the answer you’re hoping for, is it? When you’ve prayed so long, waited and hoped, and maybe even done all the “right” things to find a mate, being told to “grow where you’re planted” can feel dismissive. This advice isn’t meant to minimize your desire for love, but to redirect your focus to what God is doing in you, right now, redirecting your focus from the future or from whether you find a mate to your current life.

Perhaps one of the most limiting things you can do is to put your life on hold while you’re waiting for something to happen. Being in a waiting period can make you feel like you’re missing out or that God has forgotten you. That couldn’t be further from the truth. Just because your current reality doesn’t look like you hoped or planned doesn’t mean that it can’t be beautiful.

It’s hard to see the beauty when you’ve put a timeline on your life, thinking you have to meet a certain benchmark by a particular time. This can undermine the life God has given you. It’s tempting to look around at weddings, anniversaries, and baby announcements and feel like you’ve missed your window of opportunity, but your life is not – and should not – be defined by what you don’t have. What matters is how you choose to live with what you’ve been given.

Growing where you’re planted obligates you to invest in your life as it is today, not in the life that you’re hoping will eventually come. Build friendships, pursue dreams, serve others, and anchor your heart in God. Watch your life blossom, even without the mate you so desperately desire.

Build your own community

One of the most alluring parts of marriage for single people is often the desire for companionship and practical help. While it might feel ideal to fulfill all your needs for community in one person, you can still find your fulfillment in other ways.

God wants us to live in community and encourages us to find fellowship. Sometimes that is with a spouse, but sometimes it’s not. Just because you don’t have a spouse doesn’t mean you’re doomed to a life of solitude. You may need to be more strategic and intentional about building the kind of community that married people seem to fall into naturally, but it can be done.

Putting yourself out there might feel uncomfortable when you first initiate plans or invite people into your life. But there’s something incredibly empowering about creating your own curated support system, filled with chosen family that doesn’t hinge on one person being able to meet all your needs.

Friendships can fill in the gaps where you feel the absence of a spouse. Maybe the neighbor is handy with tools and can fix that leaky faucet like a husband would. Or maybe the nice lady at church who greets you every week can provide the occasional home-cooked meal. Maybe those kids of a single mom could use the mentoring of a chosen friend, parent or grandparent.

Being surrounded by a village of chosen relationships can fulfill you in ways that no one person ever could. Though you may not have a spouse, you have the opportunity to build many close relationships with people of diverse perspectives and varied talents.

Trust God with the timing and outcome

This may be the hardest part. Waiting for God requires that you loosen your grip on a deeply desired dream. Trusting God with faith requires that you trust God’s sovereignty, even when His timing is different than your own.

Waiting on God can sometimes feel like He is absent. There may be moments when you feel like God is ignoring your heart. But the truth is that God is not careless with your life. He isn’t distracted or playing favorites.

Remember, He’s not late. Ecclesiastes reminds you that God has “made everything beautiful in its time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11, NIV), even when that time doesn’t align with your desired schedule. Trusting Him with the timing is also trusting Him with the outcome.

The outcome is His, too. It’s particularly painful to admit that your frustration about when is often masking a deeper fear of if. What if it never happens? What if the life you’ve imagined, wanted, prayed for, envied, never actually comes to pass at all?

That can be a hard reality. Instead of blaming God for the fact that you’re single and may never be partnered or married, realize that it isn’t Him who is wrong. You may have established your own set of expectations and feel disappointed when they’re not met without ever consulting God. Did you prayerfully imagine your future, or did you simply follow after cultural norms or family expectations?

Maybe God has a beautiful life of singleness planned for you. There’s freedom in singleness. Freedom to explore who you are in Christ without having to fit into anyone else’s life or schedule. Freedom to deeply invest in friendship and family, and to be the Hands and Feet of Christ in your community. Freedom to pursue passions and callings that might have been put on hold if you were to have been married.

The Fear and Grief of Singleness as You Age

Getting older and being alone can be a scary combination. The mental load of managing a life entirely on your own, from car repairs to financial planning, is heavy, indeed. Having constant responsibilities can be both physically and mentally exhausting.

In your older years, you might be grieving. You may not be missing a specific person, like you would a departed spouse, but you might mourn a version of your life that you thought you’d be living by now. This is called disenfranchised grief, and it can manifest itself in sadness for a wedding that hasn’t happened or children you never had.

You might worry about who is going to take care of you in your old age. But the truth is, everyone goes through that fear, even those who are married. A marriage license isn’t a guaranteed insurance policy against loneliness or the future. Many married people feel incredibly alone, and many spouses find themselves trying to manage their old age alone after a partner passes away.

Navigating Your Future

You have a life to live, growing to do, and relationships to be made. God has a plan for you. Maybe it includes a love story between you and a spouse. Maybe that love story is just between you and a loving Heavenly Father.

If you’re struggling in your singleness and are feeling the strains of aging in singleness, talking with a therapist can help. A therapist can walk you through processing your emotions, teach you how to challenge negative thoughts, and give you tools to help you build your community. Best of all, Christian therapy can help you recognize that God is fully able and willing to help you live abundantly, even in singleness.

Call our office to make an appointment with one of our licensed therapists who can help you embrace your single life at any age.
