item.title: Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy: Re-opening Closed Hearts
item.description:
Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFCT) is a highly effective, evidence-based approach that has become the gold standard for couples therapy. Built on the science of attachment theory, it was developed in the 1980’s by world-renowned psychologist and couples therapist, Dr. Sue Johnson.

Johnson posited that relationship conflicts and arguments are rarely about superficial issues. Instead, they are typically driven by a deep, underlying, often subconscious fear of disconnection, abandonment, or unworthiness.

Loving connection provides the dependable web of intimacy that allows us to cope with life and live life well. – Dr. Sue Johnson

The main focus of EFCT is to help distressed couples break the negative interaction cycles fueling their distress. It does this by addressing the underlying emotional needs and attachment patterns in the relationship, providing insight into why these dynamics exist, and teaching new ways of relating to one another. This is done with the goal of fostering deep emotional healing and the formation of a secure, lasting connection.

How It Works

According to Johnson, the conflict is never about the actual matter a couple is fighting about. Couples experiencing relational distress are struggling with basic attachment issues and unhealed childhood wounds they may not even be aware of. These can include feeling helpless, worthless, unlovable, inadequate, or abandoned.

As these underlying emotions get triggered and stirred up, it causes them to enter defense mode and close their hearts to each other. The signals they send tend to be distorted and misinterpreted. They may resort to anger, for instance, to try and get a response, or shut down to cope with difficult feelings or their partner’s reactions.

Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy is specifically designed to reopen closed hearts. It addresses the emotional disconnect, decodes negative patterns of interaction, and helps partners shift. They move from defensive, guarded positions to vulnerability and reconnection. They learn to reframe their arguments from perceived personal attacks to understandable responses to a sensed lack of emotional safety.

The therapist helps partners uncover the vulnerable emotions that lie deep below the surface. Together, they identify their masked attachment needs and start to understand how their attachment-related fears of loss are affecting their relationship. This helps them begin openly sharing their vulnerabilities with their partner to seek closeness and empathy, and new patterns of interaction are developed.

As they learn to become more empathetic, responsive, and attuned to each other, this leads to greater trust, emotional intimacy, and bonding. These changes foster deeper connection and attachment security.

The Science Behind Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Our relationships are not just emotional experiences. They are deeply rooted physical processes that continuously alter our brain’s wiring.

The need for a safe emotional connection with a loved one we can depend on is biologically wired into our nervous system. It is vital to our survival during infancy and times of crisis, as well as to the maintenance of our physical and mental health.

Functional MRI studies have shown that the presence of a secure loved one has a soothing effect on the nervous system. It calms the threat response and alters its neural activity in a way that fosters emotional safety and connection. Feeling rejected, isolated, or as though you do not matter, on the other hand, has a traumatizing effect.

Relationship distress is a survival-based reaction to the loss of connection. By helping couples identify and express their core emotional vulnerabilities, Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy enables them to rewire maladaptive emotional responses and restructure emotional experiences. Then they can rebuild connection and create a sense of emotional safety and trust.

What to Expect in an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy Session

During an Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy session, the therapist observes the dynamics between you and your partner. They take an active role in helping you identify the hidden vulnerabilities beneath the surface of your behaviors that are contributing to the conflict in your relationship.

A therapist also recognizes the recurring, predictable pattern of your fights in sessions. They help you learn to view this destructive pattern – not your partner – as the enemy, and guide you through new ways of interacting that foster a safe, secure connection.

The Three Stages of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Emotions are the foundation of human relationships. They influence the way we communicate and respond to one another. When our emotions are acknowledged and validated, we feel heard and understood, and our satisfaction with the relationship is enhanced. On the other hand, when partners ignore or dismiss them, it can lead to conflict, disconnection, frustration, resentment, and destructive interactions.

EFCT consists of nine specific steps, divided into three stages, that help guide couples through a process. These steps help them become attuned to subconscious emotions and unmet needs, reprocess their distressed responses, and transform negative patterns of interaction into positive, secure attachment bonds.

Stage 1, De-Escalation (steps 1-4): In this first stage, the therapist lays the groundwork for change by tracking the way you and your partner interact. They help you become aware of your negative patterns of behavior, such as criticizing, attacking, being defensive, withdrawing, or shutting down.

They work to help you understand the deeper emotions and unmet needs that are triggering these behaviors, see how your insecurities and fears are impacting your relationship, and redefine the problem as being the negative cycle you are caught up in rather than blaming each other for it.

Stage 2, Restructuring Emotional Bonds (steps 5-7): This stage is devoted to creating a sense of security and restoring the emotional bond between you and your partner. The therapist guides you through new interactions that promote emotional engagement and move you beyond defensive reactions to more authentic communication.

In this, you learn to be vulnerable with each other, share deep underlying emotions and needs without fear of being judged, respond in supportive, empathetic ways, and engage in constructive dialogues with one another rather than destructive arguments.

Stage 3, Consolidation (steps 8-9): In this last stage, the therapist helps you and your partner integrate what you have learned into your day-to-day interactions and rehearse the skills you have developed to solidify these new patterns. You can practice comforting and connecting rather than disconnecting in the face of challenging emotions.

Specific Techniques Used in Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy

Trying to change your behaviors without dealing with the unspoken issues that lie beneath the surface of your responses is ineffective, which is why EFCT is not just about better communication. It is about helping you identify and address these underlying emotions and share them with your partner.

The following are examples of the types of techniques used to enhance emotional awareness, facilitate the expression of previously disowned needs and feelings, and encourage deeper connection, empathy, and understanding between partners to create a deeper emotional bond.

Emotionally Focused Conversations: An emotionally focused conversation is a structured dialogue that helps create an environment of empathy and compassion in which each partner is encouraged to discuss his or her thoughts and feelings without being interrupted.

Hold-Me-Tight Conversations: A hold-me-tight conversation is a guided dialogue that encourages partners to be vulnerable and share their deepest fears and needs, and talk through how they each hear the revelation. It aims to slow down the negative interactions and help the couple become more empathetic, emotionally responsive, and engaged with one another, transforming relational distress into emotional connection.

Reflection and Validation: Reflection and validation are techniques used to help couples recognize and articulate their needs and feelings by deepening their self-awareness and helping them recognize and process their hidden emotions.

Using empathic supposition, the therapist mirrors their words back to them in a clearer, more detailed way. They highlight core meanings or name emotions to help them see perspectives they may have missed, validate their experience, and reinforce its importance in the relationship.

Attachment-Focused Interventions: In attachment-focused interventions, the therapist helps partners recognize their attachment style and how it is influencing their interactions. They gain insight into their emotional responses and learn to navigate relational challenges in a healthier, more effective way.

Enactments: Enactments are role-playing exercises that help couples practice the new communication skills they have learned in a supportive, non-judgmental environment under the guidance of the therapist.

Are you interested in learning more?

item.title: Why Traditional Therapies Don’t Always Help Adults with Borderline Autism
item.description:
Have you always felt like there’s something a little different about you, but not different enough for you to know exactly what makes you different? Maybe you’ve done a good job keeping up with the world around you, even though most times you have a harder time fitting in than others.

Maybe you’ve been working hard all your life, socializing, and checking all the boxes, but it still feels like things take more effort than they should. Like social situations leave you completely drained, or unexpected noises, change, or confusion throw you off for hours or even days.

You might have even heard that there’s something called borderline autism in adults, without understanding what it is. This condition is not an official diagnosis, but it does describe real experiences people, much like you, experience every day. People in this group show some traits of autism, but not all, and because of that, traditional therapy may not always be the help you need.

Let’s break down why that happens and what can actually help.

What Borderline Autism in Adults Feels Like

Borderline Autism in Adults exists in a grey area between neurotypical functioning and a clear autism diagnosis. You may not have the signs or mirror the typical idea of someone with autism. In school, you probably did just fine, and socially, you also learned how to copy the behavior of people around you over the years, smiling when you’re supposed to, making small talk, and blending in.

However, after all these years, these seemingly simple social actions have felt harder for you than they look from the outside. Many adults with borderline autism have spent years feeling different without knowing why, having to force themselves to act neurotypical. Unfortunately, these efforts come at a huge cost, causing stress, exhaustion, and identity confusion.

You might not have had a diagnosis growing up, and no one saw what was going on because you didn’t act out. You stayed quiet and always followed the rules. As an adult, you may have been told you have anxiety, ADHD, or depression, and while that may explain some parts, it probably doesn’t explain all of it.

Small Signs That You’re Living with Borderline Autism

There are signs, however, that can help you identify what living with borderline autism might look like. Some of them are:

  • You struggle to follow conversations, especially in groups.
  • You feel uncomfortable in noisy places or crowded rooms.
  • You have a strong need for structure or routine.
  • You stay deeply focused on a specific topic or interest once you’ve started.
  • You deal with big mood swings or getting emotionally stuck over small things.

If you’ve tried therapy before and always left feeling like it didn’t really help, you’re not imagining things. Most mental health approaches are built around standard diagnoses and don’t always work for people with borderline conditions, especially with autism.

This is because traditional therapy usually focuses on fixing you. A lot of therapy is designed to change how you act so you’ll fit in better. Yet if you’re already good at masking, or pretending to be fine when you’re not, this just adds unnecessary pressure. You don’t need fixing, but rather you need support that helps you understand yourself.

Additionally, most social skills training feels unnatural. Some programs teach step-by-step responses for social situations. That might help in a textbook way, but real-life conversations aren’t scripts. If you’ve ever left a conversation feeling like you missed something, even when you said the right things, this might be why.

Likewise, medication isn’t always helpful. Doctors might give you medication for anxiety or mood swings. While that may help with some things, it doesn’t deal with your deeper issues like sensitivity to light, noise, or how exhausting everyday social stuff feels.

Therapies designed for more severe autism cases do not always adapt well to adults with borderline traits. That’s because some of these approaches do not fit the life experiences you deal with daily.

What Life Feels Like Day to Day if You Have Borderline Autism

Borderline autism can leave you socially exhausted. Even a short chat can leave you mentally wiped out. Small talk feels confusing, and group conversations move too fast. You might replay things in your head for hours afterward, trying to figure out what people meant or if you said something wrong.

It can also come with sensory issues. Certain sounds, lights, or fabrics bother you more than they seem to bother others. Maybe just a simple flicker of fluorescent lights, a tag in your clothes, or too many people talking at once can throw you off. These things are hard to explain but easy to feel.

There could also be significant mood crashes. Something small, like an unexpected change in plans or a misunderstanding, can throw your whole day off. You might not always know why you’re feeling down over something others seem to be ok with, but just know it happens.

You probably have one or two things you’re really into. Not in a casual way, but in a way that brings you comfort, focus, or joy. Other people might tell you you’re too into it or not get why you get so focused on it once you start, but it matters to you.

You might be great at your job but still feel unsure when it comes to things others seem to naturally understand, like office politics, vague feedback, or unsaid rules. It’s not that you’re bad at your job; you’re just working twice as hard to understand what others seem to pick up without thinking.

If standard therapy hasn’t worked for you, don’t give up. There are other ways to get support, ways that meet you where you are, not where someone thinks you should be.

Some Therapies That May Help

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy helps you understand and work through unhelpful thoughts, like beating yourself up after social interactions or feeling like a failure when you’re just overstimulated.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy teaches skills for handling big emotions, staying calm during stress, and setting healthy boundaries. It’s especially useful if your emotions feel intense or fast-changing.

Sensory Support involves working with a therapist who understands sensory sensitivities. They can help you slowly build comfort with difficult things, like certain textures or sounds, without pressure.

Creative Therapies include art or music therapy, which give you a way to express yourself without needing to explain everything with words. It can be a break from masking and a way to let your real self breathe.

Occupational Therapy isn’t just for physical rehab; it’s also for creating routines that work with your brain, not against it. It can help with organizing your day, managing time, and building habits that lower stress.

Routine and Adaptive Planning build structure, which is comforting to you. Life isn’t always predictable. Therapy that helps you build routines and also handle change can make a huge difference.

Support for Deep Focus helps you reimagine your ability to hyperfocus. Instead of seeing your intense interests as a problem, some therapists and coaches will help you use them to reach goals, whether that’s through a career, hobby, or creative project.

Support Groups create community with others who also live the same challenges. You don’t have to explain every detail; they just get it, and that alone can lift a huge weight off your shoulders.

You deserve support that fits you, so if other solutions haven’t worked yet for you, it doesn’t mean you’re the problem. It just means you haven’t found the right kind of support yet.

You don’t have to keep pushing through life feeling misunderstood, worn out, or like you’re faking your way through every day. The right help is out there; help that makes sense for how you actually experience the world.

If any part of this sounds familiar, it’s worth talking to someone who can help you find relief. Contact our office today to make an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our association.

item.title: How Online Bereavement Therapy Can Assist with the Grieving Process
item.description:
In a disconnected world, there is a new method for navigating grief therapy. Online bereavement has become a new avenue for individuals to navigate the process of losing a loved one. It is a hybrid of traditional mourning and the digital age. People who are grieving frequently face a paradox between needing a community and wanting to grieve alone.

The digital approach of online bereavement offers a lifeline that tailors support to those who have lost a close loved one. It is a place where faith can continue to guide hearts to hope and healing. This modern method acknowledges the evolving ways people can connect. It can also provide a space where emotional wounds can heal, even amid the chaos of loss and daily life.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

Understanding Online Bereavement

Online bereavement involves the grieving process being navigated on digital platforms such as virtual memorials or support groups. Modern life, busy schedules, and the pandemic have changed the way society as a whole grieves. There was a time when we gathered in person to commemorate the passing of loved ones. Now there is a way to share memories online.

Christian counselors can step in and help individuals process the shift to online bereavement so that no one feels as though they are alone in their pain. These counselors bring compassion through their expertise, fostering a sense of belonging in virtual spaces. This can be comforting and transformative for individuals who feel as though they are stranded in the middle of their grief and mourning.

Old grieving methods seem to be ill-fitting in today’s society. This is where online bereavement services adapt and offer forums or video calls for unique losses. This availability allows for grief to be processed so that it does not harden into despair. Though it may be unconventional, this process honors personal pathways and renders the rigid rules of grieving void. It will reveal the layers that accompany any death and meet people where they are with their grief.

Individuals are assured that the flexibility will allow them to express their sorrow at their own pace. Through written tributes or live discussions, a dynamic support network develops, allowing for a separation from traditional support systems.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction… – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, ESV

The Role of Grief Therapy

Grief therapy is transformed by online bereavement, extending its reach and using virtual sessions to connect those isolated by location or stigma. The cultural message pushes resilience, but online spaces allow raw emotion to surface. The clash between stoic expectations and inner turmoil is resolved, and trauma processing is tailored with care. Christian counselors integrate faith and offer spiritual anchors to those who have lost loved ones.

Professional Christian counselors can provide a steady hand that helps individuals find peace through prayer or scripture. These tools become vital when physical distance separates them from a traditional support system.

This approach breaks barriers and links individuals in rural areas to the support they need. Online bereavement fits into chaotic lives and eases the tension between work and morning. Christian counselors blend scripture with digital tools that prevent individuals from feeling lost in outdated practices.

Technology has enabled counselors to create accessible pathways for healing, ensuring that even the most isolated individuals can find a sense of community. This brings a sense of inclusion and hope, as well as an understanding that they may struggle uniquely, but they are not alone.

Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand. – Isaiah 41:10, ESV

Benefits of Seeking Online Healing

The benefits of online bereavement and grief therapy lie in the flexibility of online sessions. Sessions can occur at any time and align with life’s demands. The cultural silence is countered, and vulnerability is allowed to breathe. Privacy draws those hesitant about face-to-face help and creates a haven for them to share their pain. Online groups are also readily available due to the lower costs. This bridges the gap for those who are far from traditional support.

Individuals are empowered through accessibility to seek help on their terms. This reduces the stigma that often comes with public mourning, and it opens doors to healing that may remain closed under traditional grief therapy. Knowing they are in a safe space, individuals who are grieving find freedom and express their emotions, whether positive or negative.

Each of these benefits addresses isolation, enabling people to connect through stories and reducing digital divides and loneliness. It can reduce overwhelming feelings with paced guidance that allows the individual to navigate the grieving process in a way that makes sense to them. Christian counselors use online prayer or Scripture discussions to integrate faith into the healing process. This blend helps individuals avoid feeling adrift.

Christian counselors understand this and can guide individuals through the process with compassion and understanding. The virtual presence of an online counselor offers a consistent source of encouragement. This is beneficial in building resilience over time, a vital component of long-term emotional recovery.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

Spiritual Integration

Faith can enhance the online bereavement role in grief therapy. Society often splits faith and mental health, creating a conflict in the individual. Scripture is full of hope, and this reframes loss through God’s lens. Online formats connect faith communities for prayer or to understand what Scripture says about grief and hope.

Christian counselors maintain a focus on identity in Christ, which facilitates healing with mercy. Spiritual connection is essential in providing a foundation of strength and resilience. This permits individuals to lean on divine support as a process, which is comforting in the anonymity of online spaces, particularly during their grief.

Journaling and group reflection are virtual tools that root this process in grace. Faith can help prevent isolation and build strength during times of unique loss. A resolution bridges the gap between despair and belief. Christian counselors emphasize the use of spiritual tools to empower individuals during the grief process. By integrating faith and community online, bereavement reminds the individual that they are not walking the path of grief alone.

These tools can encourage deeper exploration of personal faith. This fosters a sense of community and shared purpose that sustains individuals through the darkest moments of their grief journey.

So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. – 2 Corinthians 4:16, ESV

Learn about online grief therapy

Online bereavement assists grief therapy by bridging old and new and challenging the cultural silences of what is acceptable grieving. By transforming solitude into a shared experience, online bereavement challenges the notion that mourning a loss should be a private affair. Individuals emerge transformed in a way that honors the lost loved one.

A faith-based therapy provides enduring comfort and guidance toward a renewed purpose. This transforms grief into a hopeful experience, reminding individuals that even in the midst of loss, they can celebrate the goodness of God. This transformation is a testament to the power of community and faith, leaving a legacy of love that inspires even after the initial pain subsides.

If you would like more information about online bereavement, contact your local Christian counselor today to begin your pathway to healing and connection.

item.title: Hope, Stewardship, and Therapy for Eating Disorders
item.description:
Sometimes our faith, which is meant to bring peace, gets tangled up with harmful eating habits. Spiritual devotion turns into rigid control over food, and we find ourselves trapped in a cycle where discipline becomes disordered eating. This struggle calls for spiritual wisdom and professional care so we can embrace the stewardship of the body God has given us.

Therapy for eating disorders is essential for those of us whose fake journey has been weighed down by restrictive eating and legalistic thinking. This struggle goes beyond the act of simply choosing food. It is created from cultural and religious messages linking spiritual maturity to denying physical means.

Many wrestle with the tension of wanting to honor God through discipline while feeling pressured to neglect our bodies’ needs to prove our faith. This conflict makes our faith feel like a burden and not a blessing. For many of us, the guilt of eating a simple meal can sometimes feel like a betrayal of faith. This is another lie that therapy can help us unravel as we seek to steward our bodies.

Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. – Matthew 4:4, ESV

When Faith Becomes Rules About Food

In our Christian communities, we celebrate virtues such as discipline, self-control, and sacrifice as achievements in spiritual growth. These truths are rooted in scriptures, but we have allowed them to become distorted as we apply them rigidly to our eating habits. We start with practices like fasting in an effort to grow closer to God, only to find ourselves becoming obsessed with controlling our food.

When we turn spiritual practices into a way to earn God’s approval through perfect eating, we run the risk of engaging in self-shame. Fasting is meant to deepen our reliance on God, not to create a pathway of self-punishment. Fasting should never make us feel exhausted or ashamed. This is a mindset based on a false gospel that says worth depends on dietary control, not God’s grace.

We are often caught in a false gospel, where our worth hinges on dietary control, such as our need to feel pure through starvation and avoiding entire food groups. These mindsets only leave us weak and ashamed, facing exhaustion and isolation. Through therapy, we learned to overcome this mindset and realize the way to draw closer to God is to trust His guidance in stewarding our bodies.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. – Colossians 2:16, ESV

Breaking Free from Rigid Rules

The similarities between eating disorders and legalistic faith can be striking. Both rely on earning acceptance through strict rule-following, which can create a cycle of striving, failing, and shame. This becomes an exhausting treadmill of always trying to be good enough, but never arriving, and eventually causes problems with mental well-being.

This cycle can be identified by behaviors, such as panic after eating a certain food or weeping because of a fear of failing God for eating a meal. These distorted thoughts reveal the burden that steals the peace of God and leaves us trapped in the false narrative of fasting.

When we pursue this constant effort, we find the peace that God intends for us slipping away. We feel as though we have become trapped, and we question our worth simply because we cannot meet the impossible standards for eating or spirituality. When we experience guilt due to breaking a rule, we tend to set stricter guidelines, creating a harsher cycle of striving and failing. We find ourselves slipping away from resting in grace and into exhaustion from self-punishment.

Christian counselors can offer therapy for eating disorders that will help with recognizing the distorted thoughts surrounding fasting and faith. These counselors help us understand how to build healthier relationships with food in our bodies and how faith can contribute positively. Therapy helps with healing from the struggles by replacing the rigid rules with grace-filled practices.

For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. – Ephesians 2:8-9, ESV

Healing Through Therapy

Choosing to seek therapy is a courageous step that aligns with biblical wisdom. God’s word encourages us to seek counsel and community. Obtaining Christian counseling does not mean there is a lack of trust in God. It can be seen as wisdom leading to the help we need to overcome eating disorders and strict faith rules.

Believers shouldn’t hesitate to seek therapy for fear of judgment. We should allow ourselves to feel freedom as we take a step that breaks down barriers, keeping us from healing through therapy.

Therapy for eating disorders can be complex because they affect thoughts, emotions, and physical health. The care required to treat eating disorders should address biological, psychological, and social factors. Therapy through Christian counselors can provide tools to identify the triggers, challenge harmful thoughts, and rebuild a healthy relationship with food.

Christian counseling provides a unique lens to address how faith can be misused to justify restriction. It also provides direction on how stewardship of the body can support recovery.

When we choose therapy to open doors or deeper spiritual growth, we can address eating disorders and find space to connect with God without shame. Christian counselors can help us reframe things. Biblical truths about stewardship encourage nurturing our bodies and not controlling them.

Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. – Proverbs 11:14, ESV

Reclaiming Body and Soul

Recovering from eating disorders means blending faith and therapy, not choosing one over the other. This recovery is about learning to honor our bodies as God’s temple through stewardship, not punishment. This process will challenge cultural ideas that tie spiritual strength to physical denial. It will require embracing biblical principles for caring for the body.

As we navigate this journey, we will let go of the false security that controlling food provides. It may result in grief over the loss, but true peace will be found in God’s unchanging love. Therapy will help us bridge the gap between knowing God’s grace and living a life surrounded by it. In this journey, we will encounter the unconditional love of God and realize that our actions do not have to earn it. Christian Counseling will help us align our hearts and actions with faith.

Christian counselors promote spiritual practices that support healing. These practices will include gratitude and rest while challenging the distorted use of faith. They will help individuals see their bodies as a gift rather than an enemy that must be conquered.

During the process, we will often realize that the food rules were about controlling our lives, and our restrictive eating may have stemmed from a need to feel worthy. Both of these realizations are ways that distorted thinking creates eating disorders, even when we think we’re being spiritual.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body. – 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, ESV

Finding Hope

In the struggle with eating disorders as believers, our freedom will come through seeking spiritual and professional support. We can find practical tools to heal in therapy, while our faith will provide an anchor of identity and worth. Together, these tools bring wholeness, physically, emotionally, and mentally.

As we move forward through the process, we will understand how to let go of false ideas that tie spiritual values to food restriction. We will be able to embrace stewardship, grace, and health as we find a community that supports our healing journey.

This journey is about finding God’s promise of healing as we seek it through every means He has provided. Call your local Christian counselor to start your journey of freedom from disordered eating to discover hope!
